purpose: Morphine is used to treat moderate to severe pain that other pain medicines cannot control well enough. It is often used after surgery, for cancer pain, or for serious injuries. Doctors may also use it for certain types of chronic long-term pain.
how_it_works: Morphine works by attaching to special receptors in your brain and spinal cord called opioid receptors. When it attaches to these receptors, it blocks pain signals from traveling through your body to your brain. Think of it like a lock and key — morphine is the key that locks out pain messages so you feel relief.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include constipation, nausea, drowsiness or sleepiness, dizziness, and vomiting. You may also feel confused or have difficulty concentrating. Most people experience constipation, so your doctor may recommend a stool softener or laxative while taking this medication.
warnings: Morphine can slow down your breathing, which can be life-threatening — never take more than prescribed. Do not drink alcohol while taking morphine as it can cause dangerous or fatal side effects. This medication can be habit-forming and lead to dependence or addiction; only take it exactly as your doctor tells you. Keep it locked away from children and others, and never share your medication with anyone else.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very individual and depends on your pain level and medical history. Immediate-release tablets are often started at 15 to 30 mg every 4 hours for adults. Extended-release forms like MS Contin are taken every 8 to 12 hours. Your doctor will start you on the lowest effective dose and adjust it carefully based on how you respond.
